structured_content.markdown: # Ruff ## First try **Illustrative example; not executed in this review.** [Install Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/installation/), then save this as `sample.py`: ```python import math print("Ready") ``` Run this in the directory containing the file. It checks for unused imports without changing the file or loading project configuration: ```sh ruff check --isolated --select F401 sample.py ``` Representative diagnostic excerpt, not captured output (formatting varies by version): ```text sample.py:1:8: F401 `math` imported but unused ``` The location identifies the import; `F401` identifies the unused-import rule. Remove that line and repeat the check. A clean result means this selected rule found no violation in this file. ## Use it on your project Follow the [Ruff tutorial](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/tutorial/) to configure rule selection, file exclusions, and the target Python version. Run `ruff check` for linting; `ruff format` only formats code. Start without automatic fixes so you can inspect the diagnostics. ## Fixes and limitations Ruff distinguishes safe and unsafe fixes. Review proposed changes and run your tests after applying them. Record the tool version, configuration, and preview setting for repeatable results. ## Alternatives and complements Follow the [Ruff and mypy recipe](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/) to check one project with separate lint and type reports. Pair Ruff with [mypy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/mypy/) or [Pyright](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pyright/) when you also need type checking. Consider [Bandit](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/bandit/) for a dedicated Python security-rule workflow. [Pylint](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pylint/) uses inference and supports plugins; Ruff provides built-in rule families. Their rules overlap but are not interchangeable. Before switching, compare the diagnostics and plugin requirements of your project. The [official comparison](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/faq/#how-does-ruffs-linter-compare-to-pylint) explains these differences. Use the [finding review workflow](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/) to investigate a diagnostic and verify a correction.

Other hosts have not been run for this recipe. ## Prepare an isolated environment Use Python 3.13 and the pinned Ruff 0.14.3 and mypy 1.18.2 releases. These versions are a reproducible example, not a recommendation to downgrade an existing project. The target Python version is also set to 3.13 in `pyproject.toml`. On Windows, select an interpreter and check it before creating the environment: ```powershell $Python = "python" & $Python --version ``` Expect `Python 3.13.x`. If that command is missing or reports another version, set `$Python` to your Python 3.13 executable, such as `$Python = "C:\path\to\Python313\python.exe"`, and repeat the check. Continue from `examples/python-checks` once the version matches: ```powershell & $Python -m venv .venv .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.txt ``` On Linux or macOS, use `.venv/bin/python` in place of the Windows interpreter path. Installing the pinned packages requires package-index access. The fixture has no application dependencies or service credentials. ## Check the faulty version Run both checks and keep their reports: ```powershell .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe run_checks.py bad --output reports/bad ``` The runner verifies versions, runs each tool separately, and saves commands, input hashes, host details, versions, and return codes in `run.json`. Diagnostics go in `ruff.json` and `mypy.txt`, with separate stderr files. Read both reports. Use a new output directory for each rerun; the runner refuses to overwrite earlier reports. It records setup failures and retains partial output on timeout. The expected signals are: | Tool | Expected finding | Meaning | | ---- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Ruff | `F401` for `math` | The imported module is unused. | | mypy | `arg-type` at `greeting("three")` | The argument is text, but the parameter is annotated as an integer. | The runner returns `1` when the checks complete with findings, `0` when both complete without findings, and `2` when either cannot complete. These are this runner's gate rules, not universal analyzer exit codes. Tool completion is recorded separately from the gate in `run.json`. ## Check the correction The corrected file removes the unused import and calls `greeting(3)`. Run the same configuration against it: ```powershell .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe run_checks.py good --output reports/good ``` Both reports should be clean for this fixture. The known defects and correction show that the selected checks are active. They do not measure general defect coverage or prove that the program meets every requirement. ## Use it on your project `run_checks.py` accepts only `bad` and `good`; it is a demonstration runner. For your code, run the tools directly. From `examples/python-checks`, keep the checker interpreter's absolute path, then enter your project's root: ```powershell $CheckPython = (Resolve-Path .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe).Path Set-Location "C:\path\to\YOUR_PROJECT" ``` Replace `C:\path\to\YOUR_PROJECT` with your project directory. Use its existing analyzer configuration. If it has none, add these tables to its root `pyproject.toml`, creating the file only if absent. Merge settings into any existing tables instead of replacing the file: ```toml [tool.ruff] target-version = "py313" [tool.ruff.lint] select = ["E4", "E7", "E9", "F"] [tool.mypy] python_version = "3.13" strict = true show_error_codes = true pretty = false ``` Match both target-version settings to the Python version your project supports. The fixture selects only `F401`; this starting selection adds other Pyflakes and selected pycodestyle checks. Review the [Ruff configuration](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/configuration/) for your project. If your settings live in `ruff.toml` or `mypy.ini`, use those paths in the corresponding config arguments below. The checker environment needs access to your project's dependencies and type stubs. Install the project's declared dependencies and needed stub packages in that environment, or use a project environment with the checkers installed by setting `$CheckPython` to its interpreter. Resolve [missing imports and stubs](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/running_mypy.html#missing-imports) before treating a clean result as useful type coverage. Choose one small source directory and a new report directory for this run: ```powershell $Target = ".\src\YOUR_PACKAGE" $Reports = ".\check-reports\first-run" New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $Reports -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null & $CheckPython -m ruff check --no-fix --no-cache --config pyproject.toml ` --output-format json $Target > "$Reports\ruff.json" 2> "$Reports\ruff.stderr.txt" $RuffExit = $LASTEXITCODE $RuffExit | Set-Content "$Reports\ruff.exit.txt" & $CheckPython -m mypy --no-incremental --cache-dir "$Reports\mypy-cache" ` --config-file pyproject.toml $Target > "$Reports\mypy.txt" 2> "$Reports\mypy.stderr.txt" $MypyExit = $LASTEXITCODE $MypyExit | Set-Content "$Reports\mypy.exit.txt" ``` Replace `src\YOUR_PACKAGE` with the directory you want checked. Use a different `$Reports` path for every run; stop if directory creation fails. These commands make no automatic source fixes. Read `ruff.json`, `mypy.txt`, and both stderr files with their separate exit codes. Ruff returns `0` for no findings, `1` for findings, and `2` for a failed run. A completed mypy run reports either success or a diagnostic summary; an empty report or a setup error is not a clean result. Review and correct findings, then repeat with a new report directory. Record the source revision, selected configuration, exclusions, and environment using the [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). Keep diagnostics separate; do not compare raw issue counts as measures of quality. Use the [CI result-handling guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/ci-checks/) to decide which completed findings block a change and how to retain failed or incomplete runs. ## Sources - [Python virtual environments](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/venv.html) - [Ruff rule selection and exit behavior](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/linter/) - [Ruff 0.14.3 distribution](https://pypi.org/project/ruff/0.14.3/) - [mypy 1.18.2 distribution](https://pypi.org/project/mypy/1.18.2/) - [mypy file and import scope](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/running_mypy.html) "}

item.text:
Start with Ruff for common coding mistakes, then add mypy on a small annotated part of the project. They complement each other.

| Tool | Checks | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|
| [Ruff](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ruff/) | Unused imports, common mistakes, coding conventions, and deliberately enabled security rules | Coverage depends on enabled rules; it does not replace a type checker |
| [mypy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/mypy/) | Incompatible arguments, return values, assignments, and operations using annotations and stubs | Untyped code, `Any`, missing stubs, and suppressions can hide mistakes |

Both are free, open-source static tools: neither needs to run your application.

My recommended starting sequence is:

1. **Preserve existing settings.** I found no Python checker configuration in the current workspace, so these recommendations are conditional. In your actual project, reuse its pinned tool versions, rules, targets, and exclusions.
2. **Run Ruff without automatic fixes.** For a new project with no existing lint policy, ToolWiki suggests `E4`, `E7`, `E9`, and `F` as a starting selection. Review findings before enabling more rules. Avoid casually adding `--select`: it overrides configured rule selection.
3. **Add mypy on one small annotated package.** Make the project's dependencies and required type stubs available. Start with its existing strictness; otherwise adopt checks gradually. `--check-untyped-defs` can expand checking into unannotated function bodies, while `--strict` enables broader checks.
4. **Correct findings and repeat both checks.** Keep their reports separate and continue running application tests. A clean static check does not prove runtime correctness. [ToolWiki's combined workflow](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/)

This is a documentation-based recommendation; I did not run either checker. ToolWiki's combined example has recorded Windows execution, limited to selected faulty and corrected examples.
